newsitem.title: FRANCE: French government faces tough task to cut spending.
newsitem.headline: French government faces tough task to cut spending.

text.p: The French government's bid to restore confidence with its announcement of income tax cuts last week appears to have failed and left it with a tougher task ahead of implementing spending cuts in its 1997 budget.

The government won virtually no praise for its plan, which has been called a transparent political ploy to gain votes, a gift to the rich at the expense of the poor and a contradiction with its efforts to cut its budget deficit.
A poll published on Monday showed most people believe the tax reform would do nothing to improve economic growth, employment or confidence.
"It is not a tax choice which will create an economic recovery," former finance minister Alain Madelin said.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe said last Thursday the government would cut income taxes by 75 billion francs ($14.7 billion) over five years with 25 billion applying in 1997 on 1996 income.

Less loudly trumpeted were a tightening of the tax treatment of life assurance policies, the elimination of a complicated system of tax breaks and soon-to-be-announced hikes in duties on petrol, alcohol and tobacco products.
These increases, coupled with expected higher local authority taxes, and a rise in taxes to fund the welfare system, will do much to neutralise the effect of the income tax cuts.
"There is no tax cut on aggregate," JP Morgan economist David Naude said. "You could argue that there has been a tax rise on aggregate. There is no stimulus."
With its tax plan the government has used up its room for manoeuvre without producing a shift in public opinion. It now has no more good news to offer a public already tired of austerity.
"They've shot their bolt," said UBS international economist Darren Williams. "It's a bit difficult for markets or the guy on the street to understand where the government is going."

The situation is likely to get worse after the September 18 presentation of a 1997 budget, in which the government has promised to explain how it will cut France's public deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) from a hoped-for four percent this year.
The government must hit the three percent target next year to qualify for membership of European monetary union in 1999.

To do this the government has said it will freeze 1997 central government spending at 1996's level, which is targetted at 1,552 billion francs. That implies deep spending cuts which government members have said would be about 60 billion francs.
So far the government has said how it plans to chop about 30 billion francs from outlays, but has refused to say how it will achieve the remaining 30 billion.
Economists said it is clear the government will have to use accounting tricks, some say window dressing, in a go-for-broke effort to bring the deficit in at the three percent mark.

They said such efforts, which include a 37.5 billion franc payment from France Telecom in return for taking over pension liabilities and a transfer of funds from state bank Caisse des Depots et Consignations were likely to succeed in the short-term.
But they may well be saddling the government with future liabilities which could come back to haunt France, they said.
"What they achieve in 1997 with non-recurrent items will only be temporary," Naude said. "This means increased risk for 1998."

Government officials, repeatedly questioned about how France will cut its deficit to three percent of GDP, have said observers must take the government's word that it will do what it says and promise more details on September 18.
($1=5.094 French Franc)
